title: The gold-washer
hookLine: gold refined from coarse to fine impurities, step by step (AN 3, the gold-washer)
last: ONE KIND ACT, ONE CLEAN CHOICE.

lines: A MAN WASHING GRAVEL FOR GOLD.
cards: Cleaning out a garage has an order. First the big stuff: the broken bike, the boxes of who knows what. Then the medium stuff: tools, cans, things to sort.
Then the fine stuff: dust, cobwebs, the last screws in the corner. Nobody starts with the cobwebs while the bike's still in the way.
The Buddha used a picture like that, from a trade his listeners could watch at work: someone standing in a river, washing gravel to find gold.

teach.b: Raw gold, the Buddha says, has coarse impurities: soil, sand, grit and gravel. The gold-washer pours it into a trough and rinses them away. Then the medium ones, fine grit and coarse sand.
Then the fine ones, fine sand and black dust.
What's left is gold dust. The goldsmith puts it in a crucible and blows on it, again and again. At first it isn't workable; it hasn't let go of all its dross.
At last it becomes soft, pliable and bright, ready for any ornament he wants: a ring, earrings, a chain. Then the Buddha maps it onto a person in training.
The coarse impurities are misconduct of body, speech and mind. Those go first. The medium ones are thoughts of sensual desire, ill will and harming.
The fine ones: thoughts about one's family, one's home country, one's reputation. Then even thoughts about the teaching itself, a kind of busy spiritual chatter, are let go.
And the mind becomes steady, unified and workable, like the gold. It's an honest picture of change.
The order is practical: you don't work on subtle thoughts while you're still lying to people.
And the pace is slow. Each stage gets its own washing, and even the crucible takes time. The gold doesn't come out bright until it has let go of what isn't gold.

how: Buddhist training in many traditions is taught as gradual, beginning with ethical conduct and moving to meditation and wisdom, and teachers often use the gold-washer to describe that order.

o: a miner who strikes it rich in a single day
a merchant who weighs gold to judge its worth
someone who refines gold step by step, coarse to fine

s: the gold-washer starts with the finest dust
he washes out the coarse impurities first, then the medium, then the fine.
the gold is workable as soon as it reaches the crucible
at first it isn't; only after repeated blowing does it become soft and bright.
thoughts about the teaching itself are among the last to settle
the discourse lists them after thoughts of family, country and reputation.

games.q: you're starting to train your mind, and there's a lot to work on. what does the gold-washer teach about where to start?
o: with the coarse layer: misconduct of body, speech and mind.
all at once, in one pass.
games.why: the coarse impurities go first, then the medium, then the fine. each stage gets its own washing.

practice: Choose one habit you'd like to refine, not remove all at once. Ask, like the gold-washer, what the coarse part is: maybe the action itself, the sharp word, the extra drink, the late night.
Picture washing just that layer away, and leave the finer layers, the thoughts and moods underneath, to come in their own time.

wordCard.voice: The gold-washer. In the Book of Threes, gold is washed of coarse, then medium, then fine impurities, and the mind is refined the same way, step by step. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali suvanna: gold, the metal refined in the gold-washer simile.

carryVoice: Your line: refined slowly. Nobody expects the whole riverbed to turn to gold in one pass. Day six hundred fifty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.100 (Pamsudhovaka Sutta; AN 3.101 in some editions)
